questions.prompt: Why does a zero-order hold behave approximately like a delay of T/2?
options: Because the hold halves the gain of the signal, which lowers the phase by T/2
On average the held value is T/2 old compared with the continuous signal
Because the hold samples at twice the rate, so the signal lags by half a period
Because the hold removes high frequencies, which delays the signal by T/2
questions.explanation: The hold produces a staircase that lags the underlying signal by about T/2.

questions.prompt: A pole at s = -50 and T = 0.1 s is mapped to z = exp(sT). Which statement is correct?
options: z is outside the unit circle, so the sampled system is unstable
The pole is lost by sampling, so it no longer affects the response
z = -50*0.1 = -5, which is outside the unit circle, so it is unstable
z = 0.0067 is inside the unit circle: stable, and very fast at the samples

questions.prompt: The simulated step response looks fine but a real encoder with coarse resolution leaves a constant small offset that integral-free feedback never removes. Most likely cause?
options: An unstable pole of the plant, which drifts to a constant small value
Euler instability of the discretisation, which settles on a small offset
Aliasing of the encoder signal, which adds a constant offset at low speed
Quantisation dead zone: commands near zero round to zero
questions.explanation: When |K y| < q/2 the quantised command is zero, so the loop stops.

questions.prompt: You write the motor command after sleeping the rest of the period instead of right after computing it. What is the main effect?
options: It cancels the ZOH delay, since the command is then held for less time
It adds almost one extra sample of delay and jitter, lowering the stable gain
It only affects the logging of the control signals and not the closed loop
It improves the timing, because the command is applied at the exact period edge
questions.explanation: The output is one period older than necessary.

questions.prompt: A notch at 50 rad/s is implemented with Tustin's method (no prewarping) at T = 0.03 s. At what frequency (rad/s, 2 decimals) does the digital filter actually have its notch?
questions.explanation: Tustin evaluates the analogue filter at (2/T) tan(wT/2), so an analogue feature at wP appears at w = (2/T) arctan(wP T/2) = (2/0.03) arctan(0.75) = 66.667 x 0.6435 = 42.90 rad/s, 14% low. Prewarping at that frequency would fix this one frequency only.

questions.prompt: Plant y' = -5 y + 20 u, ZOH at T = 0.05 s, law u = -K y with one sample of delay. Largest stable K (3 decimals)?
questions.explanation: Ad = e^{-0.25} = 0.77880 and Bd = (20/5)(1 - Ad) = 0.88480. With one sample of delay y_{k+1} = Ad y_k - Bd K y_{k-1}, so z^2 - Ad z + Bd K = 0. For K > 0 the Jury conditions 1 - Ad + Bd K > 0 and 1 + Ad + Bd K > 0 always hold, and |Bd K| < 1 gives K < 1/Bd = 1.130. (Without the delay the limit would be (1 + Ad)/Bd = 2.010.)

questions.prompt: Integrator y' = u with u = -K y. The command computed from the sample y_k reaches the plant 0.2 T after the sample (the old command is held until then). What is the largest stable K*T?
options: 2.000, the same as with no latency, because the hold has not changed
3.333, larger than with no latency
1.000, the one-sample-delay value, because any latency counts as a full sample
5.000, because less than half the command is delayed
questions.explanation: y_{k+1} = y_k + 0.2 T u_{k-1} + 0.8 T u_k. With x = K T: z^2 - (1 - 0.8x) z + 0.2x = 0. Jury: |0.2x| < 1 gives x < 5; 1 + a1 + a0 = x > 0; 1 - a1 + a0 = 2 - x + 0.4x > 0 gives x < 2/0.6 = 3.333. The tighter bound is 3.333. A fractional latency below T/4 raises the limit above 2 in this model, but the worst case over all latencies in [0, T] is 1.
